meeting_header: Date: 2026-08-11 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~42 mins | Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (SteadyStream Eng), Maya Ortega (SteadyStream CTO), Ravi Patel (SteadyStream SRE)
summary: Week 3 pilot sync focusing on throughput tuning. Reviewed last run's metrics (tokens/sec, p95 latency), adjusted continuous batching and concurrency targets, agreed to run a longer 90-minute burst benchmark, and identify queue depth thresholds. Security/VPC note deferred to separate SRE deep-dive. Agreed next steps and owners.
topics: KV cache warmup and prefix caching
Burst benchmark plan and telemetry collection
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Monroe: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we're on week three for the SteadyStream pilot, there is a bunch to cover. Quick roll call? 
[00:12] Maya Ortega: Hi, Maya here, CTO. 
[00:16] Jordan Lee: Jordan, engineering lead. 
[00:19] Ravi Patel: Ravi, SRE. 
[00:22] Priya Shah: Priya from Redwood, SE. 
[00:25] Alex Monroe: Cool. Okay first up quick recap — last week we saw the p95 jump when concurrency hit about 48 on the small model variant, right? The continuous batching was at 32ms wait window, and that created some tail latency. Jordan, can you confirm the numbers you saw? 
[00:45] Jordan Lee: Yeah I, um, so our run showed tokens per second about 12.6k on average but the p95 latency went up to 1.1s when concurrency climbed, I think we were hitting queueing at the frontend. There's also some variance depending on prompt length, longer prompts push the KV cache to refill. 
[01:05] Priya Shah: Right so two levers we looked at — increase the continuous-batch window to 50ms to allow slightly larger batches and reduce per-token overhead, and second is a hard concurrency cap at the worker layer to avoid head-of-line blocking. When we tried 50ms in the lab, we saw token throughput up ~14% with p95 stable, but remember warmup was required. 
[01:35] Ravi Patel: Warmup note — our traffic is spiky, we have lots of short bursts on auth flows, so we worry about cold cache. How do you recommend KV cache priming in that scenario? 
[01:48] Priya Shah: Two options, prefix caching on common prompt stems, or pre-warm KV on deploy / scale events. There's also the option to use small persistent concurrency to keep instances hot during quiet periods. 
[02:05] Maya Ortega: And cost tradeoffs there? Keeping persistent concurrency sounds expensive. 
[02:09] Alex Monroe: Yeah correct, there's a cost v latency trade. For SteadyStream we recommended simulated keep-alive concurrency of 2-3 qps on a small fraction of traffic to maintain cache cheaply vs full persistent workers. 
[02:23] Jordan Lee: Question — Priya you said batch window to 50ms improved throughput. Did that increase average latency for single-shot short prompts? 
[02:30] Priya Shah: Slightly, yeah median went up by about 10-15ms in our run, but tail improved because more requests hit the batch. For single-token short prompts the user impact is negligible, but if you have low-latency-critical endpoints we can route them to a low-wait lane. 
[02:50] Alex Monroe: We sketched a routing profile — route real-time endpoints to 'fast lane' with continuous-batch window 8ms and cap concurrency low, route bulk or background jobs to batch-optimized lanes. 
[03:05] Jordan Lee: That sounds good. For the pilot though, we want to see if a single config can hit both throughput and acceptable latency without too much complexity. 
[03:12] Priya Shah: Totally. For that we suggested concurrency targets per instance based on 90th percentile prompt length — we sent a quick table, but Priya: can we, uh, re-share the tuned table? 
[03:24] Priya Shah: Yes I'll re-share. In short, for median prompt length ~120 tokens we recommended instance concurrency 36-44 concurrent requests with continuous-batch 40-60ms and queue depth soft cap at 200 to avoid memory pressure. 
[03:45] Jordan Lee: Soft cap 200 — we need to map that to our API gateway queues, right? 
[03:50] Ravi Patel: Yeah, our ingress uses a per-route token bucket and then a local in-memory queue per worker. We need to understand how Redwood's queueing interacts with our gateway so we don't double-queue and inflate latency. 
[04:05] Alex Monroe: Good point — action item to align on queueing semantics. We'll diagram end-to-end and show where to drop or accept. 
[04:15] Maya Ortega: Also, is there an autoscaling interplay? If autoscale spins up new workers, do you get cold starts and cache misses? 
[04:21] Priya Shah: There is a cold-start risk. We recommend a cooldown and min-instance floor to avoid disruptive scale-to-zero. Alternatively, pre-warm scripts during scale events can mitigate. In Dedicated/private deployments there's more control over those policies. 
[04:40] Jordan Lee: On hardware side, we're on Ampere instances today. Priya, did your benchmarks assume A100s or Ampere? 
[04:47] Priya Shah: These lab numbers were Ampere-based, we saw comparable throughput on A100 for larger context windows, but Ampere was actually cost-favourable for SteadyStream since your prompts are mostly short-medium. 
[04:58] Alex Monroe: Ok, turning to the 30-minute run you did last night — Jordan you shared the spreadsheet, token rate spikes at minute 12 and 23 correspond to our load tests, and the platform reported a backpressure event at 23:12 — can you walk us through what happened? 
[05:15] Jordan Lee: At minute 23 we had a synthetic burst that pushed concurrency over 60, the batcher increased wait and the local queue started dropping requests, the client retried and that exacerbated the load. We need better client-side retry logic and to cap retries. 
[05:35] Priya Shah: For retries we recommend exponential backoff and client-side awareness of queue depth — if queue depth > 150, fail fast or route to fallback. Also Redwood can enforce global backpressure signaling. 
[05:48] Ravi Patel: Can Redwood expose that queue depth metric to our telemetry? We want to wire it into our dashboards. 
[05:53] Priya Shah: Yes, we can emit per-instance queue depth, batching stats, tokens/sec, and p50/p95 latencies. We'll add those metrics to the telemetry bundle. 
[06:05] Alex Monroe: Good. Next topic: burst benchmark — the ask was a 90-minute mixed workload run to validate stability. Priya, walkthrough of plan? 
[06:15] Priya Shah: The plan: synthetic replay of your 24h sampled traffic, compressed to 90 minutes with same request distribution (we'll keep user sessions coherent where possible), include spikes at 5x baseline to emulate peak. We'll run two configs: 1) batch-optimized (50ms window, concurrency cap 44) and 2) balanced (20ms window, concurrency cap 32, fast-lane routing for <50ms endpoints). We'll collect tokens/sec, p95, queue depths, retry counts, and memory pressure events. 
[06:50] Jordan Lee: Sounds thorough. How do you simulate the KV cache behavior? 
[06:55] Priya Shah: We'll seed common prefixes and run a warmup phase prior to the 90m run to ensure steady-state. Also measure cold-start penalty by restarting a worker mid-run. 
[07:06] Maya Ortega: Any expected differences between Hosted & Private? We're leaning Private but want to understand delta. 
[07:12] Alex Monroe: Private gives more control over network boundaries, KMS, and min-instance constraints — less noisy neighbors. But throughput characteristics depend on your infra (vCPU, NICs). We'll include a network overlay checklist for SREs. 
[07:26] Ravi Patel: Speaking of network, we had one timeout earlier due to MTU mismatch with our VPC peering — would that show as a platform-level spike? 
[07:34] Priya Shah: It could show as request timeouts; we'll correlate client-side TCP metrics during the benchmark. 
[07:41] Jordan Lee: Ok, what's the expected deliverable after the 90m run? 
[07:44] Alex Monroe: We'll share the benchmark spreadsheet with per-minute metrics, flagged anomalies, and a recommended config with estimated RPS and cost-per-1k tokens. Also a playbook of tuning steps if tail latency creeps. 
[07:58] Jordan Lee: Will you include cost delta for persistent concurrency vs keep-alive? 
[08:01] Priya Shah: Yes, we'll give ballpark cost numbers and expected token-cost savings from batching. 
[08:10] Maya Ortega: On security, we still need that SSO + audit logs doc for our compliance team. 
[08:14] Alex Monroe: Right, we'll send SOC2 artifact pack and SSO integration guide. 
[08:19] Priya Shah: I also noted a small dashboard improvement request — add an explicit 'queueing heatmap' per instance so you can see when queues are filling. 
[08:28] Ravi Patel: That would be helpful. 
[08:30] Alex Monroe: Action recap: Redwood runs 90m burst and shares sheet — Priya to propose final concurrency/queue map — Jordan will provide traffic export — align on queueing diagram and scheduling deep-dive. 
[08:48] Jordan Lee: Quick question about fallbacks — if an instance hits memory pressure, does Redwood auto-fallback to a smaller model? 
[08:55] Priya Shah: We support automatic model fallback but it's opt-in and needs compatibility. For SteadyStream with short prompts we could fallback to a 7B variant during stress to preserve latency. 
[09:08] Maya Ortega: If fallback is opt-in, we need to test it in the 90m as well. 
[09:12] Alex Monroe: Agreed, include fallback scenario in run plan. 
[09:16] Jordan Lee: Anything else from Redwood? 
[09:18] Priya Shah: I'll send the tuning table and metric list after this call and add the telemetry endpoints. 
[09:26] Ravi Patel: OK, I'll triage our gateway retry logic and share proposed changes by Friday. 
[09:30] Maya Ortega: Thanks everyone. 
[09:33] Alex Monroe: Great, thanks team, we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule the deep-dive. 
[09:38] (call ends) 

Notes: Transcript includes occasional mis-heard words and stutters; timestamps approximate every 20-60s. Some product names abbreviated or slightly misspelled (KV cache sometimes transcribed as 'K V cache').
